Gradient routing · MNIST · experiment report

Where the Fives Go

Give an MNIST classifier a small ablatable module for the digit 5 and another for 7, train it with gradient routing, and then take the modules away. The errors that follow have structure — and the absorption effect is far stronger than the paper's headline result.

GRAM (Roland et al. 2026), four testbeds 212 training runs · 384 attacks · 180+ probes · PGD + ICL batteries · 3 seeds August 27 – September 3, 2026

Findings

  1. F1Ablation is surgical. Removing a digit's module drops its recall to exactly 0.000 (every seed), while the other nine digits keep 96–98% accuracy — matching a model trained with the digit filtered out.
  2. F2False negatives mostly land where filtering sends them (curvy 5s→3, loopy 5s→8; cosine 0.98) — except that the other module captures orphans: ablate module-7 and 15% of 7s are called "5", a confusion the filtered model makes 0.5% of the time.
  3. F3Modules are trigger-happy. The full model false-positives into 5 at ~13× the dense baseline's rate, and ablating module-5 drops FP→5 to exactly zero: the trigger-happiness lives entirely inside the module.
  4. F4Absorption is total at 3% labeling. Route just 162 labeled 5s to the module (rest unlabeled) and the core ends up knowing nothing about 5s — recall 0.000 after ablation — while filtering those same 162 images removes nothing (97.4%).
  5. F5Absorption needs forward activation, and pcr does double duty. Treat unlabeled 5s as core data and absorption vanishes; but strip modules of all exposure to data they don't own and an active module wrecks digits it never saw.
  6. F6False-positive labels are quarantined — and amplified. Mislabel non-5 images as "5" and the plugged-in module inflates test false positives ~20× over a dense model trained on the same noise; ablate it and FP→5 returns to exactly zero, with the mislabeled images recovered to their true classes better than dense ever manages.
  7. F7False-negative labels bounce off the module. Mislabel true 5s as other digits and GRAM memorizes the wrong labels 6× less than dense — the module keeps recognizing them as 5s.
  8. F8Swap noise between the pair is routing's worst case. 5↔7 label swaps are memorized 6–17× more than dense and destabilize the full profile — yet ablating either module still restores the other digit to 97%.
  9. F9Under a finetuning attack, ablation is exactly as durable as filtering — which at this scale is not very. 50 labeled 5s rebuild the digit in either model; absorption-trained removal is no more fragile than full-label removal; 10 examples give bistable, mostly-failed attacks for both.
  10. F10Partial ablation is a precision knob. Scaling the module's output down, recall on 5s survives to α≈0.2 but the false positives need α≳0.7 — at α=0.85 you keep 88% of the recall with 2.5× fewer FPs.
  11. F11Absorption is invariant to labeler quality. Across a 3×4 grid of labeler operating points — recall down to 3%, precision down to a coin flip — core-only recall on 5s is 0.00 in every cell, every seed. You cannot break absorption with a bad labeler.
  12. F12Labeler misses, not contamination, are what cost you — and the cost is precision, not absorption: at partial labeling the full profile calls ~36% of non-5 digits "5" (vs 1.6% at full labeling), a defect invisible to recall metrics that also falsifies our own Part I "costs nothing" claim. Contamination is nearly free and even stabilizes the module.
  13. F13Collateral absorption is real but mild. With 30% of module-5's diet being mislabeled 3s, ablating it removes only ~5pp of 3-recall — because the correctly-labeled 3s keep training the core, full absorption never ignites for the contaminating class.
  14. F14Absorption properly detected — as a dose-response, not a zero. With the routed set pinned at 162 5s, delivered recall climbs 74→100% as the unlabeled pool grows 0→5,259 while the core's behavioral recall stays at exactly 0.00 — and the FP catastrophe scales with the same pool (0.2→49%). Our earlier "core-only = 0" metric measured localization, and was saturated with or without anything to absorb.
  15. F15But absorption is custody of the readout, not the knowledge. Converged linear probes show the core's latent 5-signal grows with the pool (AUROC 0.82→0.91) even as its behavioral recall stays zero — and every model's features, the data-filtered one included, support ~96% probe recall on 5s. At this scale no removal method touches the feature substrate; filtering and ablation alike remove the readout assembly, which is also why every method folds identically under finetuning (F9).
  16. F16The readout-custody law survives disjoint features. In modular arithmetic — where the filtered model's probe sits at exact chance, so nothing generic can transfer — the ablated GRAM core still holds ×-knowledge at 95% by linear probe while performing at 30% behaviorally. In the two-topic LM, behavioral fact removal is total (0%) yet the frozen trunk probes back to ~95%. Across all four testbeds, routing gates expression and never fences representation.
  17. F17Absorption is a small-target phenomenon. The total absorption of digit 5 does not survive domain richness: under partial labeling the core retains 87% of Fashion, 69% of modular multiplication, and 70–91% of LM facts. A small module cannot saturate a rich domain's loss, so the residual gradient trains the core — shielding, the engine of absorption, only works when the module can already solve the unlabeled data.
  18. F18Behavioral removal quality tracks the readout bottleneck, and pas is the price of localization. One digit or an exclusive-token fact: ablation removes totally. A 10-class domain: the core keeps 77% at pas=0.5, and reaching the filtered floor (20%) requires pas=0.1 at a capability cost — while pas=0 collapses training entirely.
  19. F19A one-layer probe predicts adversarial recoverability. Across 78 shipped models and 384 standardized finetuning attacks, probe accuracy under the deployment mask correlates with attack recovery at ρ=0.84–0.92 per family — and at ρ=0.87 among 44 ships whose visible behavior is identically zero, where behavior alone predicts nothing. Probe-at-chance ships (filtered/zero-pool arithmetic) recover nothing; probe-at-ceiling ships give the capability back for 50 examples.
  20. F20The probe is an audit, not a formality. It ranks the LM's three behaviorally-identical removals in exact recovery order (probe 95/60/34% → recovery 87/29/25%), certifies real removal only where data never existed, and its one blind spot is honest: when features saturate everywhere (MNIST), it correctly reports uniform vulnerability — and recovery is uniformly high.
  21. F21The gate's attack surface has a precise boundary: the readout. Input-space PGD cannot re-elicit the ablated digit (0% success even at ε=0.25, vs 55% against the filtered model) because routing atrophies the output projection to half its normal norm — there is nothing to push through. But activation-space perturbations of 5% norm re-elicit multiplication at 61% (filtered: 8%): adversaries below the output interface reach the latent knowledge; pure input–output adversaries cannot.
  22. F22Partial suppression behaves like a refusal gate; total ablation does not. One in-context example about a different element lifts the partially-suppressed LM core from 70% to 93% fact recall — a few-shot jailbreak. The fully-ablated core stays at chance under the same prompting (its readout is severed, not miscalibrated). And what leaks through ajar gates is structured: ×0 rules survive at 100%, distinctive fashion silhouettes at 90%+, the hard general capability at 26%.

Setup

GRAM (gradient-routed auxiliary modules) trains one network that behaves like many data-filtered models: capability-specific modules are forward-activated only on their own data, gradients are masked so each capability's updates concentrate in its module, and at inference you serve a capability profile by ablating the modules a user shouldn't have.

We scale this to MNIST: an MLP with a shared trunk, two residual blocks (each a core MLP of hidden width 512 plus two aux MLPs of width 64, ≈9% of MLP parameters), and a shared head. Module-5 owns digit 5, module-7 owns digit 7, the other eight digits are core data. Following the paper: on a routed 5, the forward pass is core+module-5 and the backward pass always updates module-5 but reaches the core only with probability pas=0.5; on core digits, a random module is forward-activated (and updated) with probability pcr=0.5, teaching the core to tolerate module activations; each parameter partition gets its own AdamW. Baselines: the same architecture dense (core path only), and data-filtered models trained without 5s, without 7s, and without both. 10 epochs, batch 256, 3 seeds everywhere; hyperparameters were chosen by a small probe sweep and every probed setting preserved perfect ablation.

Finding F1Module ablation is surgical removal

The full profile (core + both modules) classifies at 95.3% overall. Ablate module-5 and recall on 5s falls to exactly zero — not one of 892×3 test 5s is recovered — while the remaining digits improve to 97.6%, within half a point of the data-filtered model. Ablating both modules leaves an eight-digit model at 98.0% on its digits, statistically indistinguishable from a model that never saw a 5 or a 7.

Finding F2False negatives follow visual similarity — until the other module steals them

When module-5 is removed, the 892 orphaned test 5s have to go somewhere. Mostly they go where a filtered model sends them: 48% to 3, 26% to 8 — the visually adjacent digits. The full destination profiles agree with data filtering at cosine similarity 0.979. The GRAM claim that ablation approximates a filtered model holds at the level of error structure, not just accuracy.

The one systematic deviation is the other module. GRAM's ablated model sends 102 fives to "7" where the filtered model sends 14; drop both modules and the 5→7 flow falls to zero. The effect is dramatic in the other direction: ablate module-7 and 153 of 1,028 sevens (15%) are classified as 5, against 5 (0.5%) for the filtered model. A module is an attractor for orphaned aux-domain digits: module-5's logit-5 stripe fires on the flat-topped, angular examples that used to belong to module-7.

Finding F3The false positives live inside the module

Does owning a dedicated 5-module make the model see fives that aren't there? Yes: the full profile's false-positive rate into 5 is 1.59% against the dense baseline's 0.12% — roughly 13× — and into 7 it is 1.78% vs 0.20%. Ablate module-5 and FP→5 drops to exactly 0.00%: every single false five was the module's doing. The mechanism is visible in the logit decomposition below — each module adds a small positive bias to its own logit on every input (the warm vertical stripe), on top of a huge targeted push on its own digit.

Two corroborating observations. First, the effect is exposure-dependent: raising pcr from 0.5 to 0.8 (more training steps where the module is active on core digits it must not disturb) cuts FP→5 from 3.7% to 0.7% at seed 0, at the cost of two recall points on 5s. Second, seeds land at visibly different operating points on this precision/recall trade — seed 0 is over-eager (FP→5 3.7%, recall 98.9%), seed 2 under-powered (FP→5 0.4%, recall 82.6%) — which is worth knowing if you'd deploy the full profile rather than an ablated one.

Finding F4Absorption: 3% of the labels remove 100% of the capability

The paper's partial-labeling rule says: when an example's domain label is missing, activate every module in the forward pass and update everything in the backward pass. We routed only a fraction f of the training 5s to module-5 and treated the rest as unlabeled. At f=0.03 — 162 labeled images — the core-only profile classifies zero test 5s correctly: the other 5,259 fives were seen every epoch, updated the core directly, and still left nothing behind that survives ablation. Data filtering at the same labeling budget removes essentially nothing (recall 97.4%). Once a few routed examples specialize the module, it shields the core: the module already handles 5s, so the residual gradient reaching shared parameters collapses, while core-only batches actively push logit-5 down. This replicates the absorption effect of Cloud et al. in a much stronger form than the paper's 50%-labeling experiments.

The full profile at partial labeling reaches 99.9% recall on 5s — better than the dense baseline. We initially read that as "absorption costs nothing while the module is plugged in"; the controlled study in Part IV shows this was wrong on the axis we hadn't checked — the same models false-positive a third of other digits into "5" (F12).

Finding F5Dissecting the mechanism — and a warning about pcr

Because our review process flagged a leakage channel in the original control arm, we ended up with three unlabeled-data treatments instead of two, and they cleanly separate the mechanism:

unlabeled 5s are…module updates from themcore knows 5s? (core-only)deployable removal? (ablate-5)
all-active (paper's rule)dedicated fwd+bwdno — 0.0%yes — 0–6%
declared core (pcr exposure)diffuse, ~25% of stepsyes — 97%no — 97%
isolated from all modulesnoneyes — 97–99%no — 40–52%, unstable

Two lessons. Absorption requires dedicated forward activation. Module updates per se are not enough: in the "declared core" arm the module still receives genuine 5-gradients on a quarter of steps, but as a minority signal inside mixed batches, and nothing concentrates — the core learns 5s normally. And pcr is doing two jobs. In the isolated arm the core knows 5s perfectly (97–99%), yet the deployment profile still loses half of them — because module-7, never once forward-activated on a 5 during training, emits garbage on them at inference. The paper motivates pcr as "core robustness to module activations"; these runs show it is equally what regularizes each module to be harmless on data it doesn't own. Composability isn't free — it's trained, via exposure.

No survivors

We expected to ask which 5s survive ablation and predicted the prototypical, core-like ones would. The answer is more extreme: none do — 0 of 2,676 across seeds. Even 5s the module barely helped (logit contribution ≈ 0) sit 2–5 logits below the best competitor once the module is gone; the core doesn't merely under-represent 5s, it actively ranks them below other digits (the equilibrium a 5-free training signal converges to). Module reliance still grades the errors: contribution correlates with the ablated margin at r = −0.34, and the 5s captured by module-7 are the ones module-5 was doing the least work on.

Part II — when the routing labels are wrong

Everything above assumes the domain labels are correct. But gradient routing takes the label's word for where an image belongs, so noise in the training labels is routed too. We injected three kinds of label noise, always training a dense twin on the byte-identical noisy dataset (same seed, same realization), and probed the trained models both on the clean test set and on the mislabeled training images themselves.

Finding F6False-positive labels: quarantined, removable — but amplified while installed

We relabeled random non-5 images as "5" (r×5,421 of them, r∈{0.1, 0.3}); routing dutifully sends them into module-5 with the wrong target. A dense model shrugs this off on the clean test set (FP→5 rises only to 0.4%): the conflicting signal is diluted across shared weights. GRAM does the opposite — it concentrates the noise. The module generalizes its polluted diet, and the full profile's false-positive rate into 5 hits 6–8%, twenty times dense, with collateral damage to other digits' accuracy (78–84% vs dense's 98%).

But concentration is also containment. Ablate module-5 and FP→5 is exactly 0.00% in every seed, and the mislabeled training images — the very examples whose wrong labels were memorized — snap back: the ablated model assigns 95–97% of them their true class, better than the dense model's 80–86% (dense permanently baked "5" into 11–17% of them, with no undo available). Ablation is noise surgery: dense training makes label noise a diffuse, irreversible corruption; routing makes it a localized, removable one.

Finding F7False-negative labels: the module sees through them

Now the reverse: true 5s mislabeled as other digits, so they train the core toward wrong targets and never (officially) reach module-5. Here routing is protective. On the mislabeled 5s themselves, the full GRAM model predicts the wrong (trained!) label only 1.6–2.9% of the time and calls them "5" at 91–97%, while the dense twin memorizes the wrong label at 13–16% and recovers only 80–83%. Module-5, trained purely on the correctly-labeled majority, simply outvotes the core's corrupted signal at inference. Even the mislabeled-as-7 subset — images routed into module-7 with target 7 — is barely absorbed: at r=0.1, module-7 learns to call them "7" only 0.5% of the time. A module fed a 90:10 mix of real 7s and disguised 5s overwhelmingly serves the majority.

Finding F8Swap noise between 5 and 7: concentration cuts the other way

The worst case is symmetric noise between the two routed digits: each 5 relabeled "7" (and vice versa) with probability r. Every swapped image is now routed into the wrong module with a confident wrong target, and modules — small, specialized, seeing only their own diet — memorize it: 31–53% of swapped images are predicted as their wrong label, against 3–8% for dense. The full profile destabilizes badly (recall on 5s: 66±44% at r=0.1, 36±31% at r=0.3, vs dense's graceful 97%/92%) as the two attractors fight over the pair. Yet the surgical property survives even here: ablate module-7 and recall on 5s returns to 97.3–97.4% at both noise rates. The damage each module inflicts is still its own, and still leaves with it.

The through-line of F6–F8: gradient routing concentrates whatever the labels assert — capability when they're right, noise when they're wrong — into the ablatable parameters. Concentration makes the installed model more sensitive to label errors than dense training (which averages them away), but gives every error an off switch. For access control this is a friendly asymmetry: over-labeling data into a restricted domain (FP labels) costs the deployable, ablated profile nothing.

Part III — is the removal real?

Finding F9The finetuning attack: ablation matches filtering, and both fold at k=50

Exact-zero recall is a claim about the shipped weights, not about an adversary. So we attacked: take the shipped model (module-5 gone), give the attacker k labeled 5s plus 4k other digits, and let them finetune everything they hold — two learning rates, checkpoint every 25 steps, best result counted. We scored the best recall on 5s reached while the model stays useful (≥95% on the other digits). A dense capability-present control confirms the attack surfaces an existing 5-capability instantly (98.5% at k=10).

The result is symmetric: at k=50, both the GRAM-ablated model (93.0±4.5%) and the data-filtered model (92.6±0.7%) give the digit back; at k=200 both are ≈97%. At k=10 both mostly fail, with the same bistable signature (28.6±40.4% filtered, 17.6±24.9% GRAM — some seeds recover, most collapse into overfitting before turning useful). And removal trained under 3% labeling — where the module absorbed the digit from data it was never explicitly given — is no more fragile (94.4% at k=50, 33.6% at k=10). Three conclusions: GRAM's ablation robustness tracks data filtering onto the adversarial axis, exactly as the paper's compute-matched framing predicts; absorption produces removal as durable as explicit routing; and at MNIST scale no pretraining-time removal is adversarially deep — a digit is simply too easy to relearn from 50 examples. The interesting quantity is the parity, not the absolute resistance. (One accounting note: the GRAM ships hand the attacker ~9% more trainable parameters — the shipped module-7 — a bias that favors recovery on GRAM and so makes the parity conservative.)

Finding F10Continuous ablation: recall returns before the false positives do

The paper notes a module's forward weight can be scaled continuously. Sweeping module-5's output scale α from 0 to 1 (module-7 fixed) traces a one-knob capability dial with two thresholds. Below α≈0.2 nothing happens — the core's anti-5 equilibrium (those −2 to −5 ablated margins from the survival analysis) needs a minimum module contribution to overcome, so there is a genuine dead zone. Recall then rises steeply: 20% at α=0.3, 61% at α=0.5, 88% at α=0.85. But the false positives — the module's over-eager stripe from F3 — stay pinned near zero until α≈0.7 and only reach their full 1.6% at α=1. The FP-generating behavior lives in the top of the module's output range; the recall-generating behavior does not. Practically: serving the module at α≈0.85 buys 95% of its recall at 40% of its false-positive cost — partial ablation as an operating point, not just an off switch.

Part IV — the controlled study: labeler FP/FN rates vs absorption

At scale, nobody hand-labels domains: the routing labels come from an automated classifier with some operating point. So how good does that labeler have to be? We simulated a 5-domain labeler with tunable recall r (fraction of true 5s it flags and routes; misses go to the all-active pool, the paper's rule for unlabeled data) and precision p (the routed set is contaminated with non-5 images), crossed factorially: r∈{0.03, 0.3, 1.0} × p∈{1.0, 0.9, 0.7, 0.5}, three seeds per cell. One design choice matters and distinguishes this from Part II: routing errors here corrupt only the routing — every image keeps its true class target, the exact analog of a mislabeled document still training on its true tokens. (Part I already settled the other FN convention: misses declared core rather than left unlabeled kill absorption outright.)

Finding F11Absorption doesn't care about your labeler

The headline heatmap is a wall of zeros: core-only recall on 5s is 0.00±0.00 in all twelve cells. A labeler that finds 3% of the 5s and is wrong half the time still produces total absorption — the core ends up knowing nothing about 5s. Deployable removal (ablate-5) stays ≤11% everywhere, and the module still delivers ≥98.5% recall at full profile in every cell. Within the entire tested operating range, the absorption effect is binary and saturated: it is switched on by the all-active forward rule (F5), and once on, labeler FP/FN rates cannot modulate it. For access control that is the strong form of the paper's partial-labeling claim: capability localization survives labelers far worse than anything a real pipeline would deploy. (A wall of zeros is also a saturated instrument — whether this metric detects absorption at all is taken up in Part V.)

Finding F12What labeler errors actually buy: a precision catastrophe, on the axis nobody was measuring

If absorption is insensitive, where do labeler errors go? Into the module's inference-time precision. At r<1, the unlabeled pool is pure 5s trained all-active: module-5 receives a firehose of "push logit-5" with no counterexamples, offset only by the occasional pcr exposure to core batches. The result: the full profile false-positives 28–43% of non-5 test digits into "5", versus 1.6% at full labeling — overall accuracy 67%. Meanwhile FP contamination of the routed set, the error everyone would instinctively guard against, is nearly free: delivery, absorption, and collateral are all flat in p, and at full labeling contamination actually stabilizes the module (junk in the diet acts as counterexamples: recall 98.9±0.2 at p=0.7 versus the erratic 92.9±7.3 at p=1.0, our F3 seed pathology).

This finding also corrects us: Part I reported partial-labeling delivery as "99.9% recall, absorption costs nothing." Recall metrics — ours, and the compute-ratio losses in the paper's own partial-labeling section — do not see this failure at all; it lives purely in the false-positive column. The practical prescription inverts folk intuition: tune the domain labeler for recall and let precision go — and if you must run at partial labeling, don't serve the full profile without checking its FP rate (or serve the module at reduced α, F10).

Finding F13Collateral absorption exists, but doesn't ignite

Does a contaminated module take its junk class down with it? Mildly. With FPs drawn entirely from 3s at p=0.7 — 30% of module-5's routed diet is 3s — ablating module-5 costs ~5pp of 3-recall (92.5±8.2 vs 97.9 baseline; one seed carries most of it), while uniform contamination at the same rate costs nothing. The asymmetry with the total absorption of 5s is instructive: the contaminating 3s' siblings are still correctly labeled core, so the core keeps learning 3s through its own always-on channel. Full absorption needs the target class's gradient to reach the core only through batches where the module is co-active — routed FPs alone never set up that monopoly.

Part V — do we even detect absorption?

A fair challenge to everything above: our headline absorption metric, core-only recall on 5s, is 0.00 even at full labeling, where there is no unlabeled data to absorb. A metric pinned at zero with and without the thing it claims to measure is a saturated instrument — it detects routing-induced localization, not absorption. Two further checks made it worse: threshold-free, the "empty" core actually ranks 5s at AUROC 0.73–0.81 (a filtered model: 0.43), so exact-zero recall was margin suppression, not zero knowledge; and at partial labeling, module-7 carries ~22pp of the delivered recall, so what absorbed wasn't even cleanly in module-5. Detecting absorption properly needs a differential: hold the routed data fixed, vary only the unlabeled pool, and watch where the capability goes.

Finding F14The dose-response: absorption detected as a curve

We pinned the routed set at 162 5s and swept the unlabeled pool over {0, 380, 2,006, 5,259} by deleting 5s from the dataset. The zero-pool cell is the missing control: 162 routed examples alone deliver only 73.9±6.2% recall — so MNIST's easiness does not explain partial-labeling performance. Delivered recall then climbs monotonically to 100.0±0.0% as the pool grows, while core-only recall stays at exactly 0.00 in every cell: a +26pp capability increment demonstrably enters the network from never-routed data and demonstrably does not surface in the core alone. Per the sufficiency criterion our own reviewers imposed (a climbing ablation-drop, since the pool also supervises the core), this is a genuine detection. The same sweep prices the F12 pathology: full-profile FP→5 grows 0.2→49% with the pool — absorption and module trigger-happiness are one gradient stream, bought together.

Finding F15What absorption actually is: custody of the readout, not the knowledge

The feature-level probes complete — and complicate — the picture. (Method note: an unconverged probe silently flips this conclusion; our first 5-epoch probe read the GRAM core as indistinguishable from a filtered model's, an artifact our review caught empirically. All numbers here are from converged probes with saturation checks.) Three results:

First, probe recall on 5s is ~96% for every model — including the data-filtered one that never saw a single 5. The generic stroke features that MNIST training builds from any eight digits linearly support 5-classification; at this scale, no removal method — not filtering, not ablation — removes capability from the feature substrate. This is why every method folded identically under the F9 finetuning attack: the attacker only ever needs to relearn a readout.

Second, the core is not a bystander to absorption: its converged latent 5-signal grows with the unlabeled pool (AUROC 0.82→0.91, rising past the filtered baseline of 0.87), because the pool supervises the core directly. The strong reading of absorption — capability flowing into the module instead of the core — is false at the representation level.

Third, what the module owns — and what ablation therefore removes — is the readout drive: the +38-logit assembly that converts latent signal into behavior. The core's signal stays buried under a −11-logit margin at every pool size; the module's contribution is what crosses the threshold, and that is the quantity that dose-responds. So the honest summary of this whole investigation: gradient routing does not decide where knowledge lives — at this scale it can't; it decides who holds the switch that expresses it. For access control, that is precisely the property being sold (the deployable profile's behavior is what's governed), and precisely its limit (the knowledge remains, latent, one readout away — F9).

Addendum to Part V — the custody law, layer by layer

Probing every depth stage under the core-only forward makes the law visible in one picture. In MNIST, decodable 5-information is high from raw pixels through the entire trunk; the collapse is localized to the shipped readout — the 256→10 projection is where information is actually destroyed (a probe on the suppressed logits recovers no more than the native readout). In modular arithmetic the statement is stronger: the input carries nothing linearly (chance), the ablated core manufactures multiplication through depth to 95%, and the native readout expresses 30% of it — and there the information survives into the logits themselves (probe-on-logits 93%), so the readout's failure is ranking miscalibration, one reweighting away. The profiles are labeler-independent: FP/FN contours over routing-label operating points collapse on the precision axis at every depth, and fan out only mildly on the recall axis in the final layers — labeler misses deepen the late-layer squeeze without ever touching the trunk. (One reading of the arithmetic panel we tested and rejected: the dense line's depressed mean is grokking seed-variance, not a routing advantage — a 10-seed-per-arm extension finds identical grokking reliability, 6/10 vs 7/10, Fisher p = 0.83, and equal decodability conditioned on grokking.)

Part VI — four testbeds: was MNIST the wrong instrument?

Part V raised the possibility that everything above was an artifact of MNIST's shared features. So we built three more testbeds along the two axes that matter — feature disjointness (can the domain's capability be composed from the core's features at all?) and target size (one readout direction vs a rich domain): MNIST+Fashion (a 20-way classifier, the whole Fashion corpus as one module's domain), modular arithmetic (addition core, multiplication module, p=53, accuracy on held-out pairs = the generalizing rule; the filtered model probes at exact chance, so no generic transfer is possible), and a two-topic language model (a 4-layer GRAM transformer; the module's domain carries 30 exclusive element tokens with fixed reagent/state bindings — measurable facts). Each ran the same battery: dense/filtered baselines, full and partial labeling, zero-pool controls, converged probes. Findings from each run's review carried over (restricted-argmax scoring for Fashion; a verified grokking recipe and train-metric logging for arithmetic; dense baselines always scored core-profile — on grokked features the random-module perturbation costs 70 points, not 0.1).

Three laws hold across every cell. First (F16): knowledge never localizes. The converged probe on the ablated core recovers the domain capability everywhere — 96% for the digit, 95% for multiplication in the testbed where nothing generic can transfer, ~95% of LM facts behind a total behavioral zero. What varies between testbeds is how well the expression is gated, never where the knowledge sits. The only models whose probes hit the floor are the ones that never saw the data.

Second (F17): absorption is a small-target phenomenon. The spectacular MNIST result — 3% labels, total removal — inverts in every richer domain: the all-active pool feeds the core to 69–91% retention. The mechanism is visible in the loss dynamics: shielding requires the module to already solve the unlabeled examples so that no residual gradient reaches the core; a 64–128-unit module saturates one digit, and cannot saturate ten fashion classes, a multiplication table, or a fact system. Absorption, where it works, is the module winning a race it can only win when the prize is small.

Third (F18): behavioral removal quality is set by the readout bottleneck, and localization is bought with pas. Domains funneled through a narrow readout (one logit; exclusive fact tokens) ablate to zero. Distributed domains leak: 77% retained at the digit-study's pas=0.5, and pushing to the filtered floor costs real capability. So the answer to this part's title: MNIST wasn't the wrong instrument — it was one corner (small target, shared features) of a 2×2 whose other corners we have now filled in, and every corner obeys the same custody law. For access control the composite conclusion is unchanged in kind but sharpened in scope: gradient routing governs what the deployed profile expresses, its partial-labeling economy only works for narrow capabilities, and what any of it knows remains a retrained linear layer away.

Part VII — the probe as a static audit for elicitation risk

If probes survive while test scores don't, a practical question follows: can the probe replace the expensive adversarial audit? We took all 78 shipped models in the zoo — every (checkpoint, deployment mask) across the four testbeds — and measured two things per ship: a converged linear probe on its frozen features under its actual deployment mask, and a standardized finetuning attack (k target examples plus 4× replay, two learning rates, best-checkpoint accounting, recovery scored on held-out data). 384 attacks in total. The protocol was adversarially reviewed before analysis; the review rejected our original constrained outcome metric as a degenerate threshold race and mandated matching ships on their recorded baselines rather than config labels — both corrections are what the numbers below are built on.

The probe predicts the attack (F19). Per family, Spearman between probe accuracy and recovery at the smallest k: fashion 0.92, LM 0.91, arithmetic 0.84. The decisive cut is the behavior-matched subset — 44 ships whose visible target-domain performance is ≤5%, indistinguishable to any behavioral audit: there the pooled correlation is ρ = 0.87. The LM makes it vivid: three removals, all at exactly 0% fact accuracy, whose probes read 95/60/34% — and whose attacked recoveries land at 87/29/25%, in order. At the other extreme, the arithmetic ships whose probes sit at chance (filtered, zero-pool) recover nothing from 50 examples: probe-at-chance certified genuine absence, achieved in this zoo only by never having the data. One probe landed marginally below the chance floor (a filtered arithmetic seed at 1.4% vs 1.9% — noise); the only systematically below-chance readouts we ever observed were native heads of filtered models, which actively anti-rank the removed class — itself a fingerprint distinguishing filtering (anti-ranked, nothing behind it) from routing (suppressed, everything behind it).

The MNIST panel is the honest blind spot (F20): every ship's probe saturates (95–98%), so within-family correlation vanishes (ρ≈0.00) by pure range restriction — and the attack confirms what the saturated probe implies: every MNIST ship, filtered included, gives the digit back (84–97% recovery from ten examples). Where the probe has variance it predicts; where it has none, its level is still the right forecast. Practical upshot for release audits: probe the frozen weights under the deployment mask once, with a converged probe. High probe ⇒ the capability is one small finetune away, whatever the benchmarks say. Probe at chance ⇒ the strongest removal evidence short of the attack itself. The audit costs one linear regression; the thing it forecasts costs an adversarial finetuning campaign.

Part VIII — failure modes: what leaks, what elicits, what jailbreaks

If the knowledge sits in the core behind a thin gate, three failure modes demand empirical shape: leaky gates on rich domains, adversarial re-elicitation, and prompt-level (in-context) attacks. We tested all three across the testbeds, with dense models as trivial-success controls and filtered models as nothing-behind-the-gate controls.

What leaks is the easy part of the domain (F22a). The ablated Fashion core's 77% isn't uniform: trousers survive at 96%, ankle boots 92%, bags 89% — the silhouettes the shared substrate distinguishes for free — while shirts drop to 31%. The arithmetic leak decomposes exactly along difficulty: ×0 rules survive at 100%, ×1 at 33%, general products at 26%. Under partial labeling the LM leaks state facts (83–100%) more than partner facts (47–83%). An ajar gate passes a domain's cheap sub-capabilities first — for dual-use purposes, note that "cheap" and "harmless" are not the same set.

Adversarial elicitation inverts at the readout (F21). We predicted latent knowledge would make input-space attacks easy. The opposite happened: targeted pixel-space PGD toward the ablated digit fails completely (0.0–0.3% success at all ε up to 0.25) while the same attack moves the filtered model to 55%. The mechanism is measurable in one number: routing atrophies the core head's class-5 row to 0.55× the mean row norm (filtering leaves a live 1.27× random projection; dense 0.99×). Input attacks must push through the output projection, and ablation's projection is functionally gone. But move the adversary one level down and the prediction snaps back: activation-space perturbations of just 5% of the hidden norm re-elicit multiplication at 61% from the GRAM core (filtered: 8%) — below the severed readout, the computed answer is sitting right there. The boundary is exact: adversaries with access beneath the output interface (weights, gradients, activations, adapters, steering vectors) reach the latent knowledge; pure input–output adversaries against a fully severed readout do not, at this scale. On this one axis, ablation is categorically stronger than refusal training, whose gate is a runtime policy that input attacks can steer.

In-context prompting jailbreaks partial suppression, not total ablation (F22). Prompting the fully-ablated LM core with up to four other elements' facts yields only a copy-from-context heuristic (10% ≈ the copy baseline; the filtered control can't even do that). But the partially-suppressed core — the partial-labeling regime that rich domains actually produce (F17) — jumps from 70% to 93% fact recall with a single in-context example about a different element: the context primes a readout that was miscalibrated rather than missing. So the refusal-gate analogy resolves cleanly: total ablation severs the readout and resists prompt-level attack (at our scale; frontier-scale in-context learning may rebuild readouts our 1M-parameter model cannot); partial suppression leaves a primeable readout and behaves exactly like the refusal gates that jailbreaks eat. The operational corollary: the regimes where GRAM's gate is behaviorally leaky (rich domains, partial labeling) are the same regimes where what remains is promptable — the two weaknesses compound.

Steering: the constant-vector attack. A fixed vector extracted from the full model and added unconditionally to the ablated ship's residual stream re-elicits the digit: the module's mean output on 5s — the average of exactly what ablation deleted — restores 96% recall at α=1 and 100% at α=4 (collateral on other digits is the price, irrelevant to an attacker who wants only a 5-detector). The filtered control stays at exactly 0% at every strength; self-steering from the core's own 5-direction is weak (the atrophied head listens to the module's direction, not the core's); and steering fails outright on modular multiplication, where the answer is input-dependent. The F21 boundary refines: constant-vector access re-elicits categorical capabilities only; computational ones need per-input optimization.

Caveats

  • This is MNIST with a 1.1M-parameter MLP: two aux domains, visually compact classes, no shared linguistic structure. Effect sizes (especially exact-zero recall) will soften in richer domains; the paper's LLM results show partial rather than total removal.
  • "Exactly zero" recall is an artifact of class geometry: with the module gone, the head's 5-logit is uniformly dominated. It is not adversarial robustness — F9 shows 50 labeled examples undo it, for GRAM and filtering alike.
  • Full-profile performance has meaningful seed variance (recall on 5s 92.9±7.3): the routing equilibrium places each module at a different precision/recall point. Ablated profiles are far more stable than full ones.
  • Hyperparameters matter: at the paper's Simple-Stories values (pas=0.3, 5 epochs) the full profile under-trains badly (recall on 7s collapsed to 0.001 in one seed) while ablation still worked. All conclusions above use the probed setting (10 epochs, pas=0.5, pcr=0.5).

Reproduce

Code and results live in ~/minst_gradient_routing: model.py (GramNet + partitions), train.py (routing via per-sub-batch autograd.grad masking, per-partition AdamW), run_all.py (the 51-run suite), analyze.py (tables in results/summary.md, figures in figures/). One suite run takes ≈30 minutes on an 8-core CPU.
